title: Exploring Multi-Order Self-Similarity for Motion Understanding
claim: Self-similarity at successively higher orders exposes distinct motion structure, and exploiting it yields consistent gains across many benchmarks and domains.
layout: 2 panels: stacked heatmap rows left, radar chart right with colored domain arc
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a) on the left is four stacked rows with tinted rounded backgrounds. The top row shows five video frames of a hand moving a green fruit, with a red query square on the third frame. Below it are three rows of five heatmaps each, labeled 1st-, 2nd- and 3rd-Order Self-Similarity. The heatmaps use a green-to-pink palette. The 1st-order maps show a small blob around the query. The 2nd-order maps show larger coherent green regions. The 3rd-order maps show branching pink structures. Panel (b) on the right is a radar chart with eight axes, one per benchmark, each labeled with an absolute score. A blue 'Ours' polygon encloses a green 'Baselines' polygon, and red arrows mark the gain on each axis. An outer ring is colored red, blue and yellow, and a matching legend bar below names the three domains: action recognition, motion VQA and robotic tasks.
caption: High-order space-time self-similarities (STSS) for effective video understanding. (a) Given a red query, the 1st-, 2nd-, and 3rd-order STSS effectively identify motion flows, motion segments, and the layout of motion segments, respectively. (b) We leverage the high-order STSS to capture diverse aspects of spatio-temporal dynamics in videos, resulting in significant performance improvements across various domains including video action recognition, motion-centric video VQA benchmarks, and real-world robotic tasks in dynamic environments.
abstract: Space-time self-similarity (STSS), which captures visual correspondences across frames, provides an effective way to represent temporal dynamics for video understanding.In this work, we explore higher-order STSS and demonstrate how STSSs at different orders reveal distinct aspects of these dynamics. We then introduce the Multi-Order Self-Similarity (MOSS) module, a lightweight neural module designed to learn and integrate multi-order STSS features. It can be applied to a wide range of motion-centric tasks with only marginal computational cost and memory overhead. Extensive experiments on video action recognition, motion-centric video VQA, and robotic tasks consistently demonstrate substantial improvements, validating the broad applicability of MOSS as a general motion modeling module.
